1.0.0.en: Cyrus: He was born in Elam and became king there in 558 BC. He was able to conquer Media in 549 BC, then Persia in 548 BC and Babylon in 538 BC. Because of the importance of Persia he was called the king of Persia. He was courageous, gentle in his feelings and religiously tolerant, so he allowed the inhabitants of his kingdom each to worship his own god. In the first year of his reign, after his victory over Babylon, the events of this book began.

1.0.1.en: After the Jews had spent seventy years in the Babylonian captivity, the kingdom of Media and Persia was able to defeat Babylon, and its first king, Cyrus, made a proclamation by word of mouth and in writing throughout his whole kingdom, calling the Jews to return to Jerusalem. He kept a copy of these orders in the records of the royal palace, and these are the ones whose importance appeared in the days of Darius the king (Ezra 6:1). For Daniel and the elders of the Jews had shown King Cyrus that his name was written in the books of their prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah (Isa 44:28; Jer 25:12; 29:10), and that they had prophesied that Cyrus would bring the Jews back from captivity so that they might build the temple and Jerusalem. The king was greatly pleased that his name had been written in the books of the prophets for more than two centuries, and he believed in God, the God of heaven, as one of the gods. He took an interest in the return of the Jews to build the house of God, and to ask on behalf of the stability of his kingdom. It is to be noted that Isaiah prophesied the return from captivity before Jeremiah prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem and the captivity, for God gives hope to His children before the affliction.

1.0.2.en: History tells us that Cyrus took care to set up temples for the gods throughout his kingdom, to gain their favor and to secure the loyalty of the peoples to him, so that they would not rise in revolt against him. But God had put this in his heart so that His people might return to worship Him in Jerusalem.

1.0.3.en: The proclamation was made throughout the whole kingdom of Media and Persia so that it would reach all the scattered Jews, whom Assyria or Babylon had taken captive, that they might return to Jerusalem.

1.1.0.en: Cyrus felt that his victories and the expansion of his kingdom had come through the help of God, the God of heaven. God called him His anointed and commanded him to build a house for Him in Jerusalem, as the prophets had prophesied.

1.1.1.en: Cyrus sensed that God, the God of heaven, was the cause of his victories and of his taking the kingdoms of the earth. He believed in Him as a god, and this made him ready to carry out God's commandment to him to build a temple for the Lord in Jerusalem. Here one opinion holds that God appeared to him in a dream, confirming what the prophets had written, which made him say that God had charged him.

1.2.0.en: Cyrus called every one of God's people who wished to return to Jerusalem to build the temple of God, and he encouraged him that God would be with him. This is great faith and an encouragement to obey God and believe in Him. It is strange that such a feeling should come from a pagan, while it is not found in the hearts of many of God's people, who did not return from Jerusalem and preferred their material attachments in captivity.

1.2.1.en: It is beautiful that Cyrus did not force anyone to return, although he had the authority to do so, but gave them freedom, because the true worship of God is accomplished only by man's choice and his love for God. Cyrus told those returning to Jerusalem that they would go up to it, for it is built upon five hills. This signifies that the temple of God is higher than the world, and that the spiritual life requires man to rise above his material attachments in order to enter it and enjoy it.

1.2.2.en: Cyrus called Him the God of Israel because after the captivity the division between the two kingdoms of Israel disappeared and they became one kingdom. Affliction helps people give up their divisions and live in the unity of love.

1.3.0.en: Cyrus required everyone who had remained in his faith in the God of Israel and his love for rebuilding His temple, wherever his place of exile might be in the kingdom of Media and Persia, to take from those around him, whether Jews or pagans, gifts for the building and service of the temple while he was traveling to Jerusalem. He also required all the people subject to him to hasten in giving to him, saying, "let them help", because the returning Jew had no money for building the temple. In this way Cyrus supplied the expenses of building the temple from the contributions of his people. He not only permitted them, but required his people to contribute, because Cyrus cared about the building of the temple and the satisfaction of the God of heaven with him.

1.3.1.en: By this the promise of God was fulfilled, which He promised to His people by the mouth of Isaiah the prophet (Isa 10:21; 40:9; 11:11), that the remnant of the children of Israel, who would be humbled by captivity, would be saved and return to Jerusalem. For this reason Isaiah called his son "Shearjashub", that is, "a remnant shall be saved" (Isa 7:3). These gifts were among the most precious things a man can possess, namely silver and gold, then cattle and any other contributions. Cyrus required his people to give the most precious of what they had for the completion of the building of the temple in Jerusalem. It is impossible to imagine that these things could happen unless God was behind all this, and it was He who moved the heart of Cyrus to carry out His will.

1.3.2.en: These contributions and gifts resemble what the Egyptians did for the children of Israel when they went out of Egypt, but the Egyptians' gifts were given out of fear of the God of Israel, whereas here they are offerings of love for the great God, especially since the Jews were loved by the Babylonians among whom they had lived. The giving of the pagans together with the Jews for the temple of God was like the sharing of Jews and pagans in building the temple of Solomon, and all this is a type of the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, which atones for believers of Jewish origin and of Gentile origin alike.

1.3.3.en: This verse also shows the importance of cooperation. Whoever cannot go to Jerusalem should at least contribute to show his feelings toward God, for team spirit is of great benefit in accomplishing successful works.

1.3.4.en: Giving to build or renew the house of God is love and honor for Him. Do not let this opportunity pass you by, so that you may show your love for Him and enjoy His presence in the Church.

1.4.s.en: (3) The return of the vessels of the house of the Lord

1.4.0.en: We see God's care in preserving the vessels of His house for seventy years, although they could have been melted down and turned into ingots of silver and gold for the Babylonians to use. They had destroyed everything that remained in the temple of God, and they took the vessels as material objects of high value, because they were of silver and gold.

1.4.1.en: The intention of Cyrus to honor God and build His house appears in the fact that he did not only proclaim the return of his people to Jerusalem, but supported them by giving them the vessels of the house of their God.

1.4.2.en: Cyrus' giving of these vessels to God's people was one of the incentives for them to hasten their return to Jerusalem, to build the temple of God and to use its vessels in worship.

1.5.0.en: Cyrus commanded the one in charge of his treasures, Mithredath, to hand over all the vessels of the house of the Lord to Sheshbazzar, who is Zerubbabel, after he had appointed him governor of Jerusalem and Judea. So he counted the vessels and handed them over to Zerubbabel.

1.5.1.en: The verse mentions that Sheshbazzar is the prince of Judah, and Haggai (Hag 1:1) mentions that Zerubbabel is the governor of Judah, which means that Sheshbazzar is a Persian name for Zerubbabel. Sheshbazzar is a Persian word meaning joy in the midst of troubles, "whereas Zerubbabel is a Hebrew word meaning "seed of Babylon" or "born in Babylon." Ezra mentions that "Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel" (Ezra 3:2), but in 1 Chronicles 3:9 he calls him "Zerubbabel the son of Pedaiah". This is because Shealtiel was the eldest son of King Jehoiachin and Shealtiel had no children, so his younger brother Pedaiah married his wife, according to the Law (Deut 25:5, 6), and begot Zerubbabel. Thus Zerubbabel is the son of Shealtiel according to the Law, and at the same time the son of Pedaiah according to the flesh.

1.5.2.en: Jehoiachin lived a long time after the captivity in Babylon, and Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel or Pedaiah as we have mentioned, is his grandson. From this it is understood that he held a standing among his people because he was of the royal line, and perhaps for this reason Cyrus chose him to be governor over Judah.

1.5.3.en: Among the reasons that may have led Cyrus to return the vessels of the house of the Lord to his people returning to Jerusalem is that he had heard that Belshazzar, the last of the Babylonian kings, had sinned by drinking wine from the vessels of the house of the Lord, and died that same night, and Cyrus entered and took the city. So Cyrus feared God and returned the vessels of His house to His people.

1.6.0.en: Here the numbers of the vessels of the house of the Lord are mentioned, and we notice that the numbers mentioned add up to less than the total stated in (v. 11). This is because the number given in (vv. 9, 10) is of the large vessels, and the rest are the small vessels, or those that were broken because of being transported. This shows God's care for every vessel of His house, since these vessels signify His people, each one a member of His Church, and He cares for him however small he may be. If the vessels of the house of the Lord were taken into captivity and remained for many years, God has returned them to Jerusalem with honor, and He is also able to bring back His children however far they have strayed from Him, even if they have been defiled by evil. He is able to cleanse them and restore them to their first rank as living members in His house.

1.6.1.en: You are a member in the body of Christ as long as you are bound to the Holy Sacraments and the means of grace. So do not stumble because of your weakness or your sins and say that God has forgotten me, or does not hear my prayer. God cares for you and gives the small members a great standing in His Kingdom if they are faithful in their love for God and hold fast to Him. Those who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel

3.0.0.en: The seventh month is a month that includes many feasts. On its first day is the Feast of Shouting, that is, the Feast of Trumpets (Num 29:1); on its tenth is the Day of Atonement (Num 29:7); and on its fifteenth is the Feast of Tabernacles (Num 29:12). It is beautiful that the people paid attention and came to Jerusalem at the beginning of the seventh month, that is, on the day of the Feast of Trumpets, to attend to the building of the altar of God.

3.0.1.en: We see unity in the gathering of the children of Israel with one heart, that is, as one man, to build the altar of God. They were men and women, rich and poor, great and small, and their gathering had a great purpose, namely the worship of God. The length of the period between the arrival of the children of Israel in their cities and their gathering in Jerusalem is not known exactly, but it seems to have been a short period. For if they set out from Babylon in the spring, which is a suitable time for travel, which takes about three months, and the seventh month begins approximately in the second half of September, then the short period they spent in their cities does not exceed three months. This shows that the first purpose of their return from captivity was the worship of God in His temple.

3.1.0.en: The name of Jeshua the high priest is mentioned before Zerubbabel, and he was the first high priest after the captivity, because the building of the altar is a priestly work according to the details of the Law. But at the building of the temple by order of King Cyrus, the name of Zerubbabel, the Persian governor, comes first, preceding the name of Jeshua in (v. 8). Sacrifices were offered from time to time on the remains of the ruined altar after the destruction of the temple, as is mentioned in (Jer 41:1-8), but now they were restoring and preparing the altar carefully according to the text of the Law. The priests and the people began by building the bronze altar first, before the rest of the details of the temple, because by the bronze altar sacrifices can be offered and worship and religious celebrations can begin; in addition, the surrounding peoples might oppose them if they undertook the great work of building the temple, as will appear after this. Here we find the importance of spiritual leadership in the person of Jeshua and the priests, and we also find the people's obedience to them in building the altar. All this shows the strong spiritual inclination in the hearts of those returning from captivity. We see that Jeshua the high priest was the grandson of Seraiah, the last high priest before the captivity, whom Nebuchadnezzar killed when he burned the temple (2 Kgs 25:18-21). As for Zerubbabel, the civil governor of Jerusalem, he was of the line of David and one of the forefathers of Christ (Mt 1:12, 13). The beginning with the building of the altar, then the temple, signifies what Christ did when He began by offering the sacrifice of Himself on the Cross, and after this established His Church, which is founded upon the sacrifice.

3.2.0.en: It appears from this verse that the surrounding peoples were strong, so the children of Israel feared them, but they relied on the power of God, who made their return easy by the order of Cyrus. They set up the altar so that they might offer sacrifices upon it, and that it might be a support to them in completing the building of the temple, defending them before their enemies. In addition to this, the people felt that the altar was the divine power that had supported the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

3.2.1.en: Likewise, it is possible to worship at an altar before a temple is completed, but it is not possible to worship in a temple without an altar.

3.2.2.en: Besides this, the building of the temple takes a long time, whereas the building of the altar can be completed quickly. Perhaps their fear of the enemies led them to complete the easiest step, which is the building of the altar, so that they would not oppose them in the building of the temple. This indeed happened, as will appear from the following chapters. The care of the priests appears in their setting up the altar in its exact place, and this required removing stones and repairing what was ruined, so that the altar would be in its proper form.

3.2.3.en: The building of the altar proclaims two things in the heart of the people:

3.2.4.en: 1- The people's acknowledgment of their need to repent of their sins.

3.2.5.en: 2- Their faith in the forgiving power of God.

3.2.6.en: How closely are you bound to the altar? It is the greatest place in the world, where Christ gives His Body and Blood. Let your heart and your life be bound to the altar, so that you may find your satisfaction and your strength and live in peace all your days.

3.3.s.en: (2) The return of the religious seasons

3.3.0.en: It appears from (v. 6), as will come, that they kept the Feast of Trumpets, which is called the Feast of Shouting, by offering a burnt offering in it, and it falls on the first day of the seventh month. This feast is followed in the same month by the Day of Atonement, which falls on the tenth day, but they were not able to keep it, because on this feast the high priest must enter with the blood of the sacrifice into the Holy of Holies, which had not yet been built.

3.3.1.en: On the fifteenth day of the seventh month falls the Feast of Tabernacles, and they were able to keep it as it is written in the Law of Moses, that is, as it is prescribed, in which they offer during the seven days of the feast a set number of sacrifices that decreases gradually until the seventh day (Num 29:13, 17). This is what is meant in the text of this verse by the expression "the daily burnt offerings by number, according to the custom, as the duty of every day required." The rest of the rite of the feast is that they dwell in booths they make of tree branches, whether in the courtyards or on the roofs of the houses, and the eighth day is a day of solemn assembly.

3.3.2.en: The keeping of the Feast of Tabernacles after the people's return from captivity, together with the building of the new altar, reminds the people (1 Kgs 8:2) that they kept the Feast of Tabernacles at the beginning of the founding of the temple of Solomon.

3.3.3.en: The Feast of Tabernacles reminds the people of being strangers to the world and of clinging to God. This is a necessary matter that God wanted to confirm within the hearts of His people returning from captivity, that their goal in life is His worship, so that they would not be occupied with possessions and property. They did sin after this and became occupied with building their own houses, but God sent them two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, who brought them back to caring about the building of the house of God and worship in it, as will appear in this book (Ezra 5:1).

3.4.0.en: The new moons: the beginnings of the months, on which they kept feasts.

3.4.1.en: After setting up the altar, the Jews began to carry out the Law, so they offered a morning burnt offering, then an evening burnt offering every day. In this way the fire remains burning on the altar continually, and that is a type of the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, which is a perpetual atonement for those who believe in Him.

3.4.2.en: The Second Book of Maccabees (2 Macc 1:19-22) tells us that the Jews had hidden the sacred fire in a well in the days of Jeremiah, at the attack on Jerusalem. The elders who knew about this matter went and found that the fire had gone out, but they found water in the well. They took some of the holy water and put it on the burnt offering, and the sacred fire blazed up in the sacrifice on the altar.

3.4.3.en: Those returning from captivity began to celebrate the new moons and to offer sacrifices, and likewise at the religious seasons and feasts they carried out the rites and received the freewill contributions of the people offered in thanksgiving to God. Thus the service and worship returned to the temple of God.

3.5.0.en: Thus the service and the offering of sacrifices began as soon as the altar was built, which was built quickly on the first day of the seventh month.

3.5.1.en: But there is a possibility that some of the Jews had built the altar a month, or two, or more before the beginning of the seventh month, and then the Jews gathered from their cities at the beginning of the seventh month, kept the Feast of Shouting and offered the burnt offerings.

3.5.2.en: Take care to take part in the holy feasts and all the occasions of the Church, so that you may be rid of your spiritual lukewarmness, your heart may be bound to heavenly things, and you may grow in your love for God. For spiritual occasions are an opportunity to pay attention amid the crowd of life's concerns.

3.6.0.en: The masons: They are those who cut the stones from the mountain, that is, who hew them from the mountain and shape them into the form suitable for building.

3.6.1.en: The Sidonians: They are the inhabitants of Sidon, a coastal city in present-day Lebanon, which was famous for shipbuilding and fishing.

3.6.2.en: The sea of Joppa: Joppa is a Jewish coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, which in this region is called the sea of Joppa.

3.6.3.en: The Jews set about their preparations for building the temple, and with the permission of King Cyrus they began their commercial negotiations with the Sidonians, who were not subject to the Persian kingdom. They agreed with them to send the timber from Sidon to Joppa, in return for giving them silver, and food, drink and oil for the Sidonian workmen who cut the wood, as Solomon had done long ago when building the temple of the Lord (1 Kgs 5:10, 11). Silver signifies redemption. The Jews paid silver to the Gentiles so that they would bring the wood for building the temple, and this signifies that redemption came out of the Jews for the salvation of the whole world, for Jews and Gentiles, for in the temple of God both Jews and Gentiles share in the work.

3.6.4.en: The silver was collected from the Jews returning from captivity. Despite their poverty they gave the most precious of their possessions out of love for God, His worship and the setting up of His temple, in addition to the silver they collected from their loved ones who were around them in captivity, as their support for the building of the temple, as Cyrus had commanded (ch. 1:4).

3.7.0.en: To set forward: to oversee the work and supervise it.

3.7.1.en: The importing of the timber from Sidon took several months, which is the period from the seventh month in the first year until the second month in the second year of their return to Jerusalem.

3.7.2.en: It is noticeable that Solomon finished building his temple in the second month (1 Kgs 6:1), and Zerubbabel begins the rebuilding of the temple in the second month, so he completes what Solomon began, regarding the period of captivity as an incidental period that passed over the Jews as a discipline for them, while their heart was attached to the temple which they had begun to build. The name of Zerubbabel the governor comes before Jeshua the high priest at the building of the temple, because Zerubbabel was commissioned by Cyrus to build the temple, and Jeshua, who understood the details of the rites of building the temple, helped him. Zerubbabel and Jeshua set up a careful system for supervising the building of the temple, so they arranged companies of the Levites to oversee the work, so that it would be accomplished according to the prescribed rites.

3.7.3.en: The age of the Levites who began the service was thirty years, and they continued until fifty years (Num 4:3), but in cases of necessity they could begin from the age of twenty, with no maximum age if their health allowed them to bear the hardships of the work (1 Chr 23:24, 27). Henadad, one of the heads among the Levites, is not mentioned in the second chapter of this book, and this is because he may have been at that time in Jerusalem and Judea and did not go into captivity. The Levites stood to oversee the work on the house of God, that is, in the place where the house would be built, because the house of God had not yet been built.

3.8.0.en: The people rejoiced when the foundations of the temple were laid and celebrated it. The priests put on the garments of service, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, who were in charge of the praise, took their cymbals, as David the prophet had arranged for them, and the trumpet of the priests. Then the sons of Asaph began to praise God, declaring their thanks to God whose mercy endures forever, because He had had compassion on His people and had granted them to re-found their temple and have their worship accepted by Him, after a captivity that lasted seventy years. The blowing of trumpets proclaims joy and gladness, and it took place at the Feast of Trumpets and at war (Num 10:8), seeking the help of God. Here, as an exceptional case, the priests used the trumpets in joy at the founding of the temple and in seeking the help of God, so that they might be able to complete its building if the surrounding Gentiles opposed them, as will appear in the next chapter. Strong feelings filled their hearts, namely:

3.8.1.en: 1- Holy zeal and love for God whom they worship.

3.8.2.en: 2- Their joy at fulfilling the will of God and the orders of their king Cyrus.

3.8.3.en: 3- Their pride in belonging to the mighty God after having endured seventy years of humiliation.

3.9.0.en: When the elders among the priests and Levites and the heads of the fathers of the people saw the temple founded, they wept with a loud voice, for the following reasons:

3.9.1.en: 1- They rejoiced at the re-founding of the temple of God which they had seen long ago before it was burned by Nebuchadnezzar.

3.9.2.en: 2- Perhaps they remembered their sins that had brought the captivity upon them, but the mercy of God brought them back from captivity and they began to found the temple.

3.9.3.en: 3- Perhaps they felt that this house was very modest compared with the great temple of Solomon, which they had lost because of their sins, so they felt grief over the temple of Solomon that was lost.

3.9.4.en: The mingling of these feelings calls for weeping, as the feelings of joy within the prodigal son at returning to his father mingled with feelings of sorrow over his sins.

3.9.5.en: The shout of the people rose in joy at the founding of the temple, and the shouting mingled with the sound of weeping, so that the voices were heard from afar.

3.9.6.en: Your true joy is in being with God, so take care to found a house for Him within you by prayers, meditations and praise, that you may remain in joy.

3.9.7.en: The opposition of the enemies and the stopping of the building
